title: Cooling Crystallization Solvent Design
contribution: A three-page problem sheet (Austin and Sahinidis, 28 July 2014) that packages a solvent-design problem for the cooling crystallization of ibuprofen as a black-box executable. Five solubility properties go in; the percent recovery of the closest designed molecule comes out, or −1 when no molecule is found.
problem_entry: Application: design an ideal solvent for the cooling crystallization of ibuprofen. The degrees of freedom are five solubility properties (three Hansen parameters, Kow, Cw), taken to be correlated with percent recovery (p. 1).
key_idea: Black-box packaging: the executable MD 64 reads the five properties from in.txt in a fixed order, solves a molecular design problem for the closest structure and writes its percent recovery to out.txt. It returns −1 if no structure lies within a reasonable distance (p. 2).
assumptions: None stated: the text gives no input bounds, noise model, evaluation cost or known optimum (pp. 1-3; figure contents not extracted).
experiments: none (problem sheet; results are in the referenced AIChE J. 2016 paper, which was not read, p. 3)
positioning: Points to Austin, Samudra, Sahinidis and Trahan, AIChE J. 62, 1514-1530, 2016, on mixture design by derivative-free optimization in the space of component properties (p. 3).
writing: Two short sections (problem, simulator interface) and one reference. The interface is specified by file names and input order (pp. 1-3).
limits_future: Reasonable distance is not defined, and failure is signalled by a value (−1) in the objective channel (p. 2). No bounds or starting point are given in the text.

method_links.note: Weak: an application turned into a runnable test problem with a documented file interface (step 5, publish problems). That it was posted as a benchmark comes from the work list, not from the sheet.

The black box is kept: the executable makes the discrete choice of molecule by an inner design solve, and the outer search runs over five continuous property targets. The reference's title names derivative-free optimization in property space. The sheet does not say which DFO method was used.

transferable: Ship an application test problem as a file-in/file-out executable with a fixed input order and a documented failure value, so that any derivative-free solver can be wired to it without the source. Better still, return failure as a separate flag and print the bounds and a reference solution (p. 2).

quotes.text: If no structure is found within a reasonable distance from the property inputs, a value of −1 is returned.
These properties will serve as the problem’s degrees of freedom and are considered to be correlated with percent recovery, a metric used to quantify a solvent’s goodness for this process.

title: Simulation optimization: a review of algorithms and applications
contribution: Not read (WRONG-TEXT). The file supplied for S040 is byte-identical to S007's: arXiv:1706.08591v1, the updated version whose formal publication is doi:10.1007/s10479-015-2019-x, carded in c03. The 4OR 2014 text itself was not available.
coauthors: Satyajith Amaran, Bikram Sharda, Scott J. Bury (per the batch list; the 4OR text was not read)

title: Relaxations of factorable functions with convex-transformable intermediates
contribution: Relaxes a G-convex intermediate φ ≤ t as G(φ) ≤ conc G(t) and proves that the least convexifying transformation gives the tightest such relaxation. Applies this to signomials, to products and ratios of convex and concave functions and to log-concave functions. Shows gap reductions over factorable relaxations, largest when the two are combined; in one BARON example the node count falls from 99 to 11.
problem_entry: Factorable relaxations need a known envelope for every intermediate, and few multivariate envelopes exist. Can nested decompositions be replaced or enhanced by transformations that exploit convex transformability (p. 2)?
key_idea: Relax {φ ≤ t} as {G(φ) ≤ Ḡ(t)} with Ḡ a concave overestimator of the increasing function G (Prop 7, p. 6). The tightest choice is the least convexifying G* with Ḡ = conc G* (Cor 4, p. 7). Applied in §§4-7 (p. 3).
assumptions: φ continuous on a convex set, G continuous and increasing, C² for the characterization (pp. 3, 5). Bounds on φ are needed; the upper bound comes from vertex enumeration, cheap because intermediates rarely have more than ten variables (Remark 5, p. 10). Prop 14 needs nonnegative exponents and zero lower bounds (p. 21).
proof_devices: augmented Hessian ∇²φ + ρ∇φ∇φᵀ and principal-minor sign analysis to characterize G-convex and G-concave signomials and their least transformations (eq. 3, p. 5; Props 10-11, pp. 10-12)
dominance between two transformations decided by the concavity or convexity of F = G2∘G1⁻¹ (Prop 8, p. 7)
closed-form maximum-gap formulas for both relaxations and their comparison (Props 12-13, pp. 13-16)
exchange argument for the exponent pairing that minimizes the RT gap (Prop 15, p. 20)
experiments: No test library. Gap tables on chosen signomials and boxes: combining the two overestimators reduces maximum and total gaps by 55% and 29% on average (Table 1, p. 17); the RT scheme by 28% and 18% (Table 2, pp. 21-23). One BARON 9.3 example at default options and a 10% tolerance: 99 against 11 nodes and 99.83% less root gap; 85% fewer nodes at 0.001% (pp. 31-32).
positioning: Measured against a widely used factorable scheme and, in §5, against the tightest factorable relaxation, chosen by Lemma 1 (pp. 23, 33). Presented as a bridge from generalized convexity, a theory with limited applications in nonconvex optimization, to global optimization (pp. 2, 33).
writing: The body reports losses: Prop 12 has the factorable relaxation dominating (p. 14), and a counterexample and a 15% total-gap increase follow (pp. 17-18). The conclusion still says the new relaxations were considerably tighter in all instances (p. 33). The computational claim is hedged as preliminary (p. 32).
limits_future: Not yet in a solver; future work will integrate the relaxations and study convergence rate (p. 33). The more complex functional forms matter for solvers that solve nonlinear relaxations, not for polyhedral ones (p. 33). The total gap can grow for larger exponents (pp. 17-18).

method_links.note: Argues that the more complex form does not matter for a solver that builds polyhedral relaxations and solves them with robust LP codes: BARON adds supporting-hyperplane cuts at the LP solution only if they shrink the relaxation.

Relaxations are ranked by gap closed on chosen functions and boxes; time and numerical failures are not measured. The only solver evidence is node counts in one example, which the authors call preliminary.

The paper precedes the code: BARON 9.3 at default options is given an alternative decomposition instead of a switch, and solver integration is left for future work. The 2015 manual lists the paper (S159 v15.2 p. 30), but that list covers algorithms, theory and applications (S159 v15.2 p. 27), so it does not show the method was implemented.
Weak: the tightness of the relaxation depends on the bounds supplied for the intermediate (Remark 5).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: add, don't replace (intersect a new relaxation with the incumbent one when neither dominates)
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The transformation overestimator does not globally dominate the factorable one, so both are included; combined relaxations reduce gaps further; the BARON test adds G-convexity cuts to the standard relaxation.

transferable: Rank two relaxations of one function by pointwise, maximum and total (integrated) gap, with percent reductions, and report their pointwise minimum as a third entry (eqs. 9-15, pp. 9-10; pp. 17, 22).
Compare a new relaxation with the tightest version of the old scheme, not with its default decomposition (Lemma 1, p. 23).
Before claiming dominance, derive closed-form maximum gaps for both relaxations and publish the cases where the new one loses (pp. 13-18).
To test an idea inside a closed solver that has no switch for it, give the solver an alternative decomposition of the same model at fixed options and compare nodes and root gap (pp. 31-32).

quotes.text: Thus, it is mostly advantageous to include both relaxations in computational implementations.
Clearly, these are preliminary results and we do not attempt to make any conclusion about the computational benefits of the proposed relaxation in general.

title: Preface: Honoring the 60th birthday of Panos M. Pardalos
contribution: A one-page preface by the guest editors, Prokopyev and Sahinidis, dedicating a JOGO special issue to Panos Pardalos's 60th birthday and summarizing his record.
key_idea: n/a; records Pardalos's books, articles, editorships, more than 50 PhD students and 2013 prizes (p. 1)
positioning: Credits Pardalos with helping to make global optimization a central activity in OR and mathematical optimization. Thanks the authors, referees, publisher and editor-in-chief Sergiy Butenko (p. 1).
writing: Conventional dedication: record, students, honours, thanks, congratulations (p. 1).
limits_future: n/a; hopes the papers will stimulate research in global optimization and its applications (p. 1).

quotes.text: Panos has helped to establish the field of global optimization as a central activity in operations research and mathematical optimization.

title: A combined first-principles and data-driven approach to model building
contribution: Adds first-principles constraints in predictor-response space to ALAMO's best-subset regression: response bounds, relations among responses, derivative and convexity limits, wider enforcement domains and boundary conditions. They are enforced by a two-phase semi-infinite method whose maximum-violation subproblem BARON solves globally. On 120 generated problems the constrained models predict and extrapolate better, at higher training error.
problem_entry: Modelers choose between first-principles and empirical models. Earlier constrained regression acted only in coefficient space, which ties a constraint to one functional form, and no work related predictors to responses (pp. 2-4).
key_idea: Constraints f[x, ẑ(x;β)] ≤ 0 for all x in X (eq. 1, p. 2), independent of the model's form (p. 4). Phase I fits on a finite set; Phase II solves the maximum-violation problem globally with BARON and returns up to n_viol separated violators per round (pp. 7-9, Algorithm 1). All of this sits inside ALAMO's MIQP with corrected AIC (pp. 5-6, 23).
assumptions: For linear-in-β models Phase I stays linear; Phase II is nonconvex and needs a global solver (p. 7). Bounds must be theoretical limits (p. 16), and derivative constraints need differentiable models (p. 18). Convexity is imposed by det(H) ≥ 0 (eq. 9, p. 20). Beyond 1-D that is necessary but not sufficient for a PSD Hessian (card-writer's check, not in the paper); the worked example is 1-D (p. 28).
proof_devices: semi-infinite termination test: β in Ω(X) iff the maximum over x of f[x, ẑ(x;β)] is at most 0, certified by a global solve of Phase II (pp. 4-5, 8)
experiments: x⁵ illustration (test EF 48.9 against 1, pp. 10-11). Batch reactor: 7.25x lower test error, then 55.2x and 7.61x with the wider domain (pp. 23-26). Convexity: −24% test error at +10% training error (p. 28). 4-D logistic: 7 against 2 terms, range [−1.35, 4.62] against [0, 1] (pp. 30-31). 120 generated problems with cumulative error-factor plots: constrained best or tied in 48% in-domain, unconstrained lowest training error in 87%, wider domain best in 58% and 60% of extrapolation tests (pp. 32-36). Cost in Table 12 (p. 36).
positioning: Extends the parameter-space restrictions of Rao, Bard and Korkhin (p. 3). In semi-infinite programming, replaces the multistart violation search of Žaković and Rustem with branch-and-reduce (pp. 7-8).
writing: Calls BARON's Phase II answer a guarantee of rigorous global optimality (p. 8), stronger wording than the skill's global-within-tolerances rule. Reports results as profiles of an error factor EF = RMSE_m/RMSE_best (pp. 11, 34).
limits_future: More re-solves and iterations, more again for wider domains (p. 36). The general multi-response case conflicts with ALAMO's per-output treatment and is handled by a sequential adaptation (pp. 16-18). No external baseline; the test set is generated (pp. 32-33). The conclusion claims applicability up to regularized regression, which is not tested (p. 37).

method_links.note: The source of step 4: bounds and physical relations are imposed during fitting and certified over the whole domain by a global solve. Constrained models are smaller when data are scarce, and limits have the greatest impact when little initial data is available.
Implemented and evaluated inside ALAMO, the test platform, by running the same data sets with the feature off, on and extended.

A profile-style comparison over a 120-problem library, but the library is generated from three function families. There is no external competitor and no structurally new hold-out family; the hold-out is new points and extrapolation domains of the same functions.

transferable: Write domain knowledge as constraints on the model output over the input domain (bounds, sums, monotonicity, curvature), not on its coefficients, so that it survives a change of basis functions (p. 4).

Enforce for-all-x constraints by discretize-and-certify: fit on a finite set, solve the maximum-violation problem globally, add several mutually separated violators per round, and stop when none remain (pp. 7-9, 11).

Compare model-building variants by an error factor EF = RMSE/RMSE_best, and plot the fraction of problems within each EF separately for training, in-domain test and each extrapolation domain (pp. 11, 34).
Test extrapolation on purpose: enforce limits over a wider domain than the data and validate on points drawn from the extension (pp. 21-22, 25-27).

quotes.text: To our knowledge, there has been no investigation into the enforcement of a priori information that directly relates predictors to regressors.
We propose a method that is similar to (b), but we employ a branch-and-reduce optimization solver—instead of a multistart local search—to guarantee rigorous global optimality.

title: BARON user manual v. 15.6. 5
contribution: Version read: v15.2 (BARON user manual of February 27, 2015), in place of v15.6.5. It sets out the user contract (finite bounds on nonlinear expressions, allowable functions), the .bar language and the termination and status vocabulary. It describes the features (NumSol, IIS, complementarity, multistart mode, parallel MIP) and all options with defaults, and ends with a 37-item bibliography.
problem_entry: n/a (manual): how to state a model so that BARON can return global optima, guaranteed under assumptions that include finite bounds on nonlinear expressions (p. 1).
key_idea: Branch and bound enhanced with constraint propagation and duality-based range reduction (p. 1); LP/MIP and NLP subsolvers (p. 3). User levers: bounds, branching priorities, relaxation-only and convex equations, starting point (pp. 6-7). Features in §6 (pp. 15-20).
assumptions: Allowed functions: exp, ln, x^α, β^x, products and ratios; no trigonometric functions (pp. 3, 5). If finite bounds cannot be inferred, global optimality may not be guaranteed (p. 3).
experiments: none (manual): a sample log for gear.bar with per-component times and cut counts (pp. 9-11), and a robot example that finds all 14 solutions (p. 18)
positioning: A bibliography of 37 BARON-related publications from 1995 to 2015 that describe the implemented algorithms, their theory and applications (pp. 27-30). Every run asks users to cite Tawarmalani and Sahinidis 2005 (p. 9).
writing: Reference-manual style. The status vocabulary separates solved within tolerances from not guaranteed and names missing bounds as the cause (pp. 12-14).
limits_future: Demo limited to 10 variables, 10 constraints and 50 nonlinear operations (p. 2); no trigonometric functions (p. 3); printed bounds may be invalid when bounds are missing (p. 12); DeltaTerm is nondeterministic (p. 20); no duals at non-KKT points (p. 15). Defaults: EpsA 1e-6, EpsR 1e-4, MaxTime 1000 s, one core, AllowFilterSD 0 (pp. 20-22, 26-27).

method_links.note: Every form of range reduction is on by default (TDo, LBTTDo, MDo, OBTTDo), and the number of probing problems is decided automatically (PDo = −2). Sampling local minima without reduction requires switching four options off, so reduction is a switchable unit.

Node relaxations are LP/MIP with outer approximators of convex functions, and MIP relaxations take most of the time on integer problems. The NLP subsolver is chosen, and switched, by problem characteristics and solver performance. FilterSD is excluded from automatic local-search selection by default, though the sample log lists it. The skill dates FilterSD's switch-off to 2022.1.19; this file cannot show what changed in between.

Every run prints the version and build date with a citation request; the log gives time per component and cuts per class; the bibliography lists the publications behind the implemented algorithms. Heuristic 2 (bounds and declarations, pp. 3, 7), Heuristic 6 (nondeterminism flagged, p. 20) and Heuristic 7 (status vocabulary, pp. 12-14) are also evidenced.

transferable: End every solver run with a small fixed status vocabulary that separates solved within tolerances from feasible but not proven, and names the missing ingredient, such as missing bounds (pp. 12-14).
Print the version, build date and a per-component time breakdown in every log, so that an ablation or a bug report can name the build and the component (pp. 9-11).
In the documentation of any option that depends on CPU or wall-clock time, say that it is a source of nondeterminism (p. 20).

quotes.text: Even though relaxation bounds are printed on the screen to give the user a feeling for convergence, these bounds may not be valid for the problem at hand.
Because it relies on CPU time measurements, which depend on machine load, this option may result in nondeterministic behavior.

title: Innovative computational tools and models for the design, optimization and control of carbon capture processes
contribution: A six-page ESCAPE-26 paper on the CCSI FOQUS toolset (SimSinter, Turbine, ALAMO, DFO, UQ, D-RM Builder, data management), shown on a solid-sorbent capture system. ALAMO surrogates fix the superstructure topology and DFO with heat integration tunes 23 variables; UQ screening, a reduced dynamic model and NMPC follow.
problem_entry: Energy technologies take up to 15 years from laboratory to pre-deployment and 20-30 years to industrial scale; the CCSI toolset aims to shorten this (p. 1).
key_idea: FOQUS links commercial simulators to ALAMO, DFO, UQ and reduced-model tools (pp. 2-3). In the case study, a surrogate-based superstructure fixes the discrete configuration, then simulation-based DFO with heat integration runs on the detailed models (p. 4).
assumptions: n/a (tool paper); lumped sorbent kinetics, a flexible BFB model and 90% capture (p. 3).
experiments: Case study: 3-stage adsorber and 2-stage regenerator (p. 4); efficiency 31.0%, 32.1% with heat integration, against 42.1% without capture (p. 4); 14 uncertain parameters screened to 6, COE most sensitive to carbamate kinetics (pp. 4-5); reduced-model validation error below 0.4%, R² 0.9954 (p. 5); NMPC residual 0.007 against 0.019, maximum control time 3.43 s within the 10 s sampling interval (p. 5).
positioning: A DOE CCSI toolset paper. It cites ALAMO (Cozad et al. 2014, 2015) and Chen et al. 2015 for heat integration (pp. 2, 6).
writing: Framed as a list of four numbered capabilities, repeated in the introduction and the summary (pp. 1-2, 5-6); no limitations section.
limits_future: No limitations stated. The superstructure solver is not named (p. 4), and DFO's advantages are listed without its lack of optimality guarantees (p. 2).

method_links.note: The design has discrete configuration decisions, and the detailed models cannot be used directly for superstructure optimization. So ALAMO surrogates settle the topology, and DFO tunes the detailed models once it is fixed (Method 3 steps 1 and 7). A 14-author paper; Sahinidis's part is not stated.
The group's tool ships as the ALAMO module of the sponsor's FOQUS framework, not inside the group's own code base.

transferable: Split a design problem with discrete topology and expensive simulations into two stages: surrogate-based superstructure optimization for the configuration, then simulation-based DFO on the detailed models with the configuration fixed (p. 4).
coauthors: David C. Miller, Deb Agarwal, Debangsu Bhattacharyya, Joshua Boverhof, You-Wei Cheah, Yang Chen, John Eslick, Jim Leek, Jinliang Ma, Priyadarshi Mahapatra, Brenda Ng, Charles Tong, Stephen E. Zitney

quotes.text: The process models include considerable details and cannot be used directly for superstructure optimization.

In particular, DFO solvers usually find a good solution even if they do not converge to a global optimum and may be suitable for noisy functions or functions where the calculations may occasionally fail.

title: Innovative computational tools and models for the design, optimization and control of carbon capture processes
contribution: A 32-page chapter with the same title, case study and tables as H006. It describes each FOQUS module in detail: ALAMO with information criteria, adaptive sampling and constrained regression; DFO plugins with heat integration; UQ; OUU with BOBYQA; D-RM Builder; the APC Framework. Its case study runs per-unit ALAMO surrogates into a MINLP of about 1000 variables, then CMA-ES with heat integration, UQ with counts of converged samples, a reduced model and NMPC.
problem_entry: As in H006, plus requirements on the models (flexible, accurate over the whole space, dynamic because plants cycle hourly). Capture at scale is outside commercial experience, so heuristic and evolutionary synthesis is argued to be inadequate (pp. 1-3).
key_idea: FOQUS modules (pp. 3-14). ALAMO selects models by information criteria (corrected AIC, BIC, Mallows' Cp) through integer optimization, samples adaptively by DFO and supports constrained regression (p. 7). Per-unit surrogates are assembled into a superstructure MINLP (p. 17).
assumptions: DFO in FOQUS needs bounds on all decision variables, used for scaling, and handles inequality constraints by a penalty (p. 8).
experiments: Per-unit ALAMO surrogates and a MINLP of about 1000 variables and equations give the same configuration as H006 (p. 17). CMA-ES on 23 variables; cooling water falls from 886.8 to 465.8 MWth (p. 18). UQ: 338 of 510 and 9648 of 10,000 samples converged; MARS is weak at high COE (pp. 19-21). Reduced-model validation error below 0.12%, R² 0.9997, against H006's 0.4% and 0.9954 (p. 26; H006 p. 5). APC table as in H006 (p. 28).
positioning: Cites the group's ALAMO papers [30], [34] and Rios and Sahinidis [33] for DFO methods (p. 7), and Caballero-Grossmann and Henao-Maravelias for surrogate-based superstructures (p. 6).
writing: A module-by-module tutorial, with typical workflows given for D-RM Builder and the APC Framework (pp. 11-12, 14). Some claims are stated without caveat: adaptive sampling outperforms LHS (p. 7); the superstructure is rigorously solved to optimality (p. 17).
limits_future: DFO gives no optimality guarantees and cannot handle large mixed-integer problems (pp. 7-8); MARS is weak at high COE (p. 21); the MINLP solver is not named (p. 17). The summary states no other limitations (pp. 28-29).

method_links.note: States the division of labour of step 1: DFO cannot handle mixed-integer superstructure problems, so algebraic surrogates let the superstructure be solved to optimality. ALAMO selects models by an information criterion through integer optimization.

Restates without caveat that adaptive sampling outperforms Latin hypercube sampling. The skill records that ALAMO's adaptive sampling was effectively disabled by a bug until 2020.4.25 and that random sampling stayed the default until 2024.10.19 (Workflow E checkpoint). The claim is attributed to Cozad et al. in a 13-author chapter.
ALAMO ships as a module of the sponsor's FOQUS framework.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: ALAMO was applied to each piece of equipment separately, so that simulations converge more often and fitting is simpler; an algebraic MINLP of about 1000 variables and equations was then assembled and solved. Attribution is weak (13 authors).

transferable: Fit surrogates unit by unit and assemble them in the optimization model: unit simulations converge more often and each fit is smaller (p. 17).
Report how many sampled simulations converged (338 of 510; 9648 of 10,000) before giving any UQ statistic (pp. 19-20).
When a response surface is still used for sensitivity analysis, say where it is weak (MARS at high COE) (p. 21).
coauthors: David C. Miller, Deb Agarwal, Debangsu Bhattacharyya, Joshua Boverhof, Yang Chen, John Eslick, Jim Leek, Jinliang Ma, Priyadarshi Mahapatra, Brenda Ng, Charles Tong, Stephen E. Zitney

quotes.text: While DFO solvers often provide good convergence to a global optimum in many cases, they do not provide optimality guarantees.
Cozad et al. [30] demonstrated that this adaptive sampling step outperforms classical Latin hypercube sampling by requiring far fewer measurements while producing more accurate models.
